# Nitric acid (aqua fortis) (`nitric_acid`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: needs distillation, saltpetre_production; helped by sulphuric_acid, glassmaking
- Core idea: Saltpetre distilled with dried green vitriol and alum (roughly equal weights) in a clay or glass retort gives red fumes that condense to a fuming acid; saltpetre with oil of vitriol (Glauber) gives it stronger and cleaner. It dissolves silver, copper and mercury but not gold, so it parts gold from silver and tests coins. It is also the gateway to explosives, dyes and nitrate fertiliser.
- Pitfalls:
  - The red-brown fumes are poisonous; the lungs can fill with fluid hours after an exposure that seemed mild. Work outdoors or under a draught.
  - Strong acid on straw, sawdust, turpentine or cloth can start fires.
  - Expecting it to dissolve gold; that needs aqua regia.
  - Stains skin yellow and burns deep; iron and copper vessels are destroyed.
- History: islamic: 8th–10th c. – attributed to Jabir ibn Hayyan in older literature; no clear recipe is known in authentic Arabic texts, so the attribution is disputed; europe: c. 1300 – first clear recipe in pseudo-Geber, De inventione veritatis; 15th–16th c. routine in assay offices and mints; 1648 Glauber's method with oil of vitriol; 1902 Ostwald process from ammonia; india: 16th c. – mineral acids described in alchemical texts; used for parting in Mughal mints
- Read:
  - William R. Newman, The Summa Perfectionis of Pseudo-Geber (1991)
  - Robert P. Multhauf, The Origins of Chemistry (1966)
  - Vannoccio Biringuccio, De la pirotechnia (1540)
